en: *Jieshu fayin shiyi* (The Elucidation of the Hidden Meanings of the Commentary on the Precepts), by the junior monk Zhuhong of Yunqi Monastery. Volume One.
The Rule of Uniformity:
When Cao Can of the Han succeeded Xiao He as Chancellor, he made no changes to any affairs, strictly adhering to He’s regulations.
The common people sang: "Xiao He governed, as uniform as a single stroke; Cao Can succeeded him, maintaining it without loss. (The character for "uniform" is 畫).
It means straightforwardness; it means clarity; it also means being orderly and well-arranged.

During the Chen dynasty of the Liang and Sui periods, the Great Master expounded upon the title of the *Lotus Sūtra* and lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts at Waguan Temple. At Guangzhai [Temple]...

The temple lectured on the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, the Crown Prince received the precepts from the Master in the Jincheng Hall;
his dream was in accord with the Master’s own hand-to-hand reception of the transmission.
When the Great Master was eighteen years old, he left the household life at Guoyuan Temple in Xiangzhou.

One day, he dreamed that there were ten thousand layers of rocky cliffs, with clouds and the sun at his side and the vast blue sea beneath him. On the mountain peak stood a monk who beckoned him to come up, leading him by the hand as he ascended.
Upon waking, he told others, "This is Mount Tiantai. The Master then set out for it and encountered Meditation Master Dingguang. Guang said to the Master:
He said, "Do you remember the time in years past when we joined hands with a beckoning of the fingers?

At that moment, the auspicious resonance caused the bells to toll, and the sound of the bells was heard filling the valley. The assembly all marveled at this strange occurrence. Guang said to the Master, "The bell is for summoning those with whom we share a karmic affinity."
"You should abide in this auspiciousness. While the *chimei* (goblins) were vanishing in anticipation of his virtue, the Master proceeded to Mount Huading.
There he practiced solitary meditation and the *dhūta* austerities. Suddenly, during the late night, a great wind uprooted trees and thunder shook the mountains.
Thousands of hosts of *māṇavaka* spirits, appearing in a hundred forms and myriad shapes, were able to cause his mind to settle in profound, tranquil emptiness.

Furthermore, they manifested in the forms of parents, teachers, and monks; yet he contemplated only the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and they soon vanished. He remained unmoved by either harsh or gentle conditions.

While a foreign monk descended from the sky to pay homage as the Master was lecturing on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, he suddenly saw three jeweled staircases in the air, spanning like a rainbow bridge. Dozens of foreign monks,
each holding an incense burner in their hands, descended the stairs and entered the hall to pay respectful obeisance.

To propagate the sutras, he went to the north of Fulong Mountain by Luoshui. This was the source of the Luo Creek; the ground was level and the springs were clear, and the location was spacious and open. The Master then settled there.
A divine being appeared and presented a written petition, saying: "I request that you, Master, practice the Way here."
When he manifested his passing at Shicheng, the Sui Emperor repeatedly issued edicts inviting him. Reluctantly complying, the Master traveled to Shicheng and said, "The Great King summoned me;
I have come because I did not wish to fail my word. Now I know that my life is here; there is no need to proceed further. Thereupon, he manifested his passing.

When the Great Master Zhi completed the conferral of the precepts upon Emperor Yang, he remarked, "Your Majesty has condescended to follow the sacred prohibitions; this may be called 'Total Retention' (Dhāraṇī).
The Emperor replied, "The Great Master transmits the lamp of the Buddha-Dharma; you shall be known as 'The Wise One' (Jñānācārya)."

"Submitting one's person with reverent devotion" (*weizhi qiānggōng*). The *Zuǒzhuan* states: "To register one’s name and submit one’s person. "Submitting one’s person" means to bend the knee; it means to surrender one’s body. Yu Rang said:

"Since I have already submitted my person to become a minister. Mencius said: "A commoner does not transmit his person to become a minister. The character *zhì* (質) is read as *zhì* (至). It refers to the person.

"Zhi" (質) means "to respond to" or "to meet with. To offer one's person as a pledge to a ruler means that it is no longer one's own possession. Furthermore, "zhi" is synonymous with "zhi" (贄), meaning a formal gift.
To hold such a gift and present it to a ruler is to enter the ranks of a subject. According to another interpretation, "wei zhi" (委質) refers to surrendering one's physical form.
Dharma Master Kumārajīva was residing in Kucha. Former Qin’s Fu Jian dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry, Lü Guang, to invade Kucha and invite the Master.
Upon reaching Liangzhou, he heard that Fu Jian had already passed away and that Later Qin’s Yao Xing had launched an invasion of Liang. Consequently, he escorted the Master to Chang’an.

In his youth, the Master could recite thirty-two thousand words daily. He followed his mother into the monastic life and traveled extensively throughout the Western Regions, where he mastered a vast array of scriptures.

He was particularly adept at the Mahāyāna teachings. Later, he resided in the state of Qin and extensively expounded upon the sūtras and śāstras. The ruler of Qin served him as his teacher, treating him with exceptional favor and honor.
The *Zhizhang* (Pointing at the Palm) quotes the *Analects*: Someone asked about the explanation of the *di* sacrifice. The Master said, "I do not know it.
One who knows its explanation would govern the world as if looking at something right here. He pointed to his palm. "Pointing to the palm" means that it is clear and easy.
The Story of Śibi Replacing the Pigeon:
In the past, there was a Bodhisattva who was a great king named Sarvada. He bestowed gifts upon sentient beings, granting them whatever they sought.

Śakra, wishing to test him, commanded a border king to transform himself into a pigeon, while he himself transformed into a hawk to pursue it. The pigeon, terrified, threw itself [into the king’s lap].
"O King, alas! My life is at its end. The King said, "Do not fear; I shall now save you.
When the hawk arrived, it said to the King, "The pigeon is my food; I pray that Your Majesty will return him to me. The King replied, "The pigeon has come to me for refuge."
"Having already accepted his refuge, I am satisfied with this. The hawk said, "I desire only the dove, not any other flesh.
If Your Majesty is compassionate and benevolent, and truly takes pity on living beings, then cut from your own flesh an amount equal to the dove's; I shall joyfully accept it.

The King immediately cut the flesh from his own thigh and weighed it against the dove's, but the dove's flesh remained heavier. He continued cutting the flesh from his body until it was exhausted, yet [the weight] still...
[The king] was not yet equal [to his vow]. He commanded his close attendants, saying: "Kill me quickly and weigh my body against that of the pigeon.

I uphold the Buddha’s precepts to rescue sentient beings from suffering and distress; though there be the afflictions of various evil spirits, they are like a gentle breeze—how could they move Mount Tai?
The hawk and the king, perceiving his resolve, remained steadfast in the Way without wavering. Each returned to its original form and prostrated themselves upon the ground, causing the heavens to...
The Medicine King applied medicinal ointment to the king’s sores, and in an instant they were completely healed. The two kings circumambulated him three times to the right and departed with joy.
(In the *Fuxing*, it is recorded that the Buddha was formerly a king named Śibi; a heavenly bird was transformed to test him. According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, this refers to Śibi.)

Regarding "Puming Quanshin" (Universal Radiance’s Complete Faith): In the past, there was a king named Puming. His compassionate benevolence shone far and wide, and his excellence was sung of throughout the ten directions.

In a neighboring kingdom, there was a king named Buzu who constantly delighted in eating human flesh; he had vowed to capture a thousand kings to offer as sacrifices to a mountain deity. King Puming went forth and observed...

The people suffered and lamented. They were seized by Baka-pāda. The king wept bitterly, grieving that since his birth he had maintained truthful speech and promised to rescue the people, yet now he had violated his word.
Baka-pāda released him. Upon returning to his kingdom, the king performed great acts of charity and installed his crown prince on the throne.
He then went forth to meet his death. Baka-pāda was moved to realization.
Regarding the King Kali’s Severing [of Limbs]:
Formerly, there was a bodhisattva known as the Rishi Kṣāntivādin who was practicing the Way in the mountains. King Kali entered the mountains to hunt;

becoming weary, he fell asleep. His consort went together with him to pay homage to the rishi. When the king woke up, he followed her to the rishi’s location and asked whether she had attained the four fruits of the śramaṇa.

They all replied, "We cannot. The king then proceeded to cut off the Bodhisattva’s limbs; the rishi endured it with patience, showing not even the slightest rise of anger, but instead gave rise to compassion.

The Prince Mahātyāga sought the *cintāmaṇi* jewel by bailing out the ocean and raining down treasures to relieve the poor. Having obtained the jewel, it fell back into the sea; he then set about bailing the ocean to retrieve it.

He said, "Though my sinews and bones may break and waste away, I shall never grow weary or desist. The devas assisted him in the bailing, and the seawater was reduced by half. The nāgas feared that the ocean—
Qian sent the pearls back to him.
When Śaṅkha was in the fourth dhyāna, his inhalation and exhalation had ceased. A bird, thinking him to be a log, laid its eggs in his topknot while he remained in meditative concentration.
He arose with the intention to walk, fearing he might damage the eggs, and immediately entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Only after the bird had departed did he arise.
King Śrīghoṣa divided the cities, towns, mountains, and rivers of Jambudvīpa into seven portions; they were distributed equally and sufficiently for each. Once—
There is no deficiency. By means of this, disputes are stilled.

Within the progression of the two [truths], there are two kinds of Middle Way: namely, the "mere" (but) and the "not-mere" (but-not). If one perceives the mere Middle, one is met by the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha/śrāvaka); if one perceives the not-mere [Middle], one is met by the Perfect Teaching.

In the interim, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) comes to provide a transition. Furthermore, those who receive this transition differ according to their three levels of capacity: those of superior capacity are transitioned at the third or fourth stage;

those of middling capacity, at the fifth or sixth stage; and those of inferior capacity, at the seventh or eighth stage. Regarding the teachings by which they are transitioned, there is a distinction between the "semblance" and the "true.

If one is transitioned while in a semblance stage, it corresponds to the tenth stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśanirdeśa*) in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), or the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching. If one receives the transition while in a true stage, it corresponds to the [tenth stage] in the Distinct Teaching...
The First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) corresponds to the Perfect First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*).

Regarding the hexagram *Dui* (Joy) from the *Book of Changes*, which depicts the mutual enrichment of two marshes, it says: "Marshes adorning each other form the hexagram *Dui*. The noble person, accordingly, uses this as a model for friends studying and discussing together" (two marshes adorning one another mutually benefit each other; friends...).
[The text] discusses this. Its imagery is as follows). Regarding the precepts for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) states:
"If you are caught in the net of fame, the hair-ropes of gain and offerings, and the tree of gathering followers, you should..."
"Push it away early. Do not receive it, do not cling to it.
Both Zhiyi (Tai) and Huisi (Heng) said, "One must diminish oneself.
Tiantai said, "If I did not lead a community, I would surely purify my six sense organs; because I diminished myself for the sake of others, I have only attained the fifth stage."

Nanyue said: "In this life, I hoped to enter the stage of the Bronze Wheel [Cakravartin]; yet, having led disciples too early, I have only attained the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties.
[This concludes] the Three Norms and Four Practices.

Entering the chamber of the Tathāgata’s compassion, donning the robe of the Tathāgata’s patience, and sitting upon the seat of the Tathāgata’s dharma-emptiness—these are called the three modes of practice.
Physical conduct, verbal conduct, mental conduct, and the practice of compassion are called the four practices of peace and bliss.

There was once a person who gave rice to a dog, while another offered rice to the Buddha. The Buddha divided the rice and gave it to a starving dog, saying, "The merit of these two acts is equal and no different."

King Gou of Yue poured out his wine when he was about to attack Wu. When someone presented him with a gift of strong wine, he ordered it to be poured into the river and commanded the soldiers to drink from the downstream current;
thus, the entire army became intoxicated.

The *Miaozong* (Exquisite Commentary) states: "To reach the bottom of ignorance and arrive at the limit of all phenomena is called 'limit-reaching wisdom' (*prāntakoṭi-jñāna*); it is the inconceivable wisdom of skillful means.

Now, in this *Fayin*, I shall present an alternative interpretation: the phrase is "reaching the source and bottom of ignorance as the limit. Although [this reading] is minor, it is not without merit.
The same. The general meaning is identical.

The eight recollections are: first, recollection of the Buddha; second, recollection of the Dharma; third, recollection of the Saṃgha; fourth, recollection of the precepts; fifth, recollection of relinquishment; sixth, recollection of the devas; seventh, recollection of... [text ends].
Inhalation and exhalation; the eight recollections; death.
When Tian Dan was leading his army to attack Di, he went to see Lu Zhonglian. Zhonglian said, "General, you cannot take Di."
Furthermore, when Tian Dan was attacking Di, he could not achieve victory for three months. He then questioned Zhonglian, who said:
"When you, General, were at Jimo, you sat cross-legged amidst the straw bales and stood leaning on your spade, leading the soldiers by example.
At that time, you possessed a heart set on death, while the soldiers had no thought of living; this is why you defeated Yan. Now, General, to the east you have the night..."
As for the support of the village, there is the pleasure of the banks of the Zī River to the west. With golden girdles fastened across their waists, they gallop between the Zī and the Shèn rivers.
Possessing the joys of life and lacking the intent for death—this is why they cannot be overcome.
Shen Yao, the Gaozu of Tang, could not take Hebei with all the world;
yet with a mere company of soldiers, he took the empire. When it reached the time of Emperor Daizong, Hebei rebelled and could never be pacified.
Therefore it is said that one cannot take Hebei with the greatness of the whole world; this means merely—
His breath was failing.
He threw himself to feed a tiger.

Long ago, there was a Bodhisattva of resolute mind who constantly dwelt in mountains and marshes, single-mindedly and diligently contemplating the Way. While traveling to seek wild fruits and melons, he encountered...
A tigress, lacking food, desired to devour her cubs. The Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with compassion; looking in all directions, he found nothing with which to feed the beast.
He then cast himself down to provide sustenance for her.
The Split-Backed Whole Deer:
In the past, the Bodhisattva was the king of a herd of deer, providing universal protection for his flock. When a herdsman reported this to the King, the King led his troops to surround them.
As the deer king was on the verge of tears, he said to the herd: "I shall sacrifice my life to save you, my small followers."
The Deer King then lowered his two front legs and said, "Mount me and leap forth. The herd of deer followed his example, and all were saved.
The Deer King’s body was torn open, and blood flowed, covering the ground.
Regarding the account of the Bodhisattva feeding the people by breaking his own body into pieces: in former times during a year of famine, the Bodhisattva transformed himself into a great fish.

He commanded the starving people to cut off and eat his flesh, saying to them, "You need only refrain from ending my life. If you should end my life, my flesh will rot and decay, making it difficult for me to sustain you for long."
"O you who do not take life, my flesh shall remain preserved for a long time, sufficient to sustain you until the harvest is ripe.
[End of Volume Two] The Three Matters in Which Jambudvīpa Excels
1. The power of severing lust; 2. the power of mindfulness; 3. the power of diligence. One [commentary] says these three Buddhas were all born from these [powers].
Regarding the passage, "If I were granted a few more years, at fifty I would study the *Yi* (Book of Changes); by doing so, I could avoid great errors," the commentary states: "Fifty..."
The character "十" (ten) appears to be a variant of "卒" (final). This is because at this time, Confucius was already sixty years old.

Although the seed of Buddha-nature is universally possessed by all sentient beings, it is produced through the precepts; thus, it may also be called a "seed. As it is said: "The seed of Buddhahood..."
This refers to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The *Avataṃsaka*, *Pāramitā*, and *Nirmāṇarati* [Sūtras] do not mention it, whereas this sūtra does. In the *Avataṃsaka*, it was taught in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*) that there are ten types of patience (*kṣānti*); this sūtra...
This is explained within the Second Dhyāna.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the assemblies at the Flower Treasury World and the Universal Radiance World differ in their seating arrangements and the stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*) vary; the ten concentrations are taught first with reference to the stages (*bhūmi*) and subsequently as concentrations (*samādhi*). This sutra, however, was taught in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
The ten concentrations: first the concentrations, then the stages.

Regarding the similarities and differences among the three teachings in the South, this refers to the masters of the various schools in the South. They do not possess the gradual teaching, because they claim that in the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*, the Great [Vehicle] was taught immediately after six years. This concludes the section on non-returning.
It is fixed; it is not for this reason that [the Buddha] does so now, because he acts solely for the sake of the Mahāsattvas.

As for the "original fixed body" (dharmakāya), its nature is fundamentally fixed, meaning it is unchanging and immovable. Śākyamuni has already realized the three bodies (trikāya); he manifests the recompense body (saṃbhogakāya) once again.

When Vairocana preaches the precepts and the Nirmāṇakāya Śākyamuni receives them, this does not contradict the statement in this sutra that Vairocana preaches and Śākyamuni receives [the precepts] (Śākyamuni’s doubts are here explained; let it remain for further examination).
The eight masteries of the sovereign self are:
first, the ability to manifest one body as many bodies, their number equaling that of motes of dust; second, filling the great trichiliocosm with a body the size of a mote of dust;

third, traveling great distances with ease while in a massive body; fourth, manifesting infinite forms while constantly residing in a single land; fifth, the mutual functioning of the sense faculties.
Sixth, attaining all dharmas as being like non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*). Seventh, reciting a single verse for immeasurable eons.
Eighth, the body being like empty space, appearing and disappearing according to circumstances without end.
The Azure Emperor (Qingdi) is compassionate and benevolent;
spring belongs to the East, its color is azure, and he who presides over the generation of spring is named the Azure Emperor.
The people of Yue are divine and sagely.
Bian Que was a native of Bohai Commandery during the Spring and Autumn period. His surname was Qin and his given name was Yue-ren. He was a man of divine sagacity. The Medical Classics state:

"To know [a disease] by observing the complexion is called 'Divine' (shen); to know it by hearing the voice is called 'Sage' (sheng); to know it by questioning for symptoms is called 'Skilled' (gong);
to know it by feeling the pulse is called 'Artful' (qiao)."

There are mountains coming from the four directions, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. As I once told King Prasenajit: "Suppose four great mountains were to come from the four directions, intending to harm the people.
What plan would you devise, O King? The King replied, "World-Honored One, even if they were to come, there would be no place to escape; only..."

"You should single-mindedly maintain the precepts and practice generosity. I then praised him, saying, "Excellent, Great King! What I call the 'four mountains' are precisely the birth, aging, sickness, and death of sentient beings."
The *Rākṣasa-kaivarta-nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Suppose there is a person in the world who wishes to cross the great ocean and obtains a single life-preserving float. He guards it with single-minded devotion.
A rākṣasa says to him, 'I beg you for this entire float. The man does not comply. [The rākṣasa] begs for half; [he] begs for as much as a hand."
He was asked for as much as a finger’s breadth; he was asked for as much as a single mote of dust. In all such cases, he did not comply.
A bhikṣu who guards the pure precepts is likewise like a life-preserving float. He must not grant even a single mote of dust’s worth of cause for breaking the precepts to the rākṣasas of affliction.
If there is even the slightest impairment, one will be unable to cross the great ocean of birth and death.

Regarding the screening of obstacles and the repeated inquiry for one who comes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*): first, one asks about the thirteen grave obstacles and the sixteen minor prohibitions; only if these are absent does one confer the precepts.
Lower the butcher’s knife.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a butcher named Viśālakarman who slaughtered countless sheep every day.
Upon meeting Śāriputra, he turned his mind toward the Dharma and received the precepts; he laid down his butcher’s knife and declared, "I am counted among the number of the thousand Buddhas."
When the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging saw the fourfold assembly, he would always speak to them, saying, "I do not disparage you;
you shall all become Buddhas. Having heard this, the people reviled, slandered, and abused him. Because of these causes and conditions, he fell into the Avīci Hell.

Regarding the methods of filial support, the *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) states: "In serving one's parents, there should be concealment [of their faults] but no offense. Attending to them from left and right for their nourishment is without fixed method.
To be "without fixed method" means that at every location and at every moment, one ought to provide support; what specific place or time could there be?
The *Shangshu* says: "It is simply recorded in the heart of God Most High" (*jian* means to examine; when a person possesses goodness, it is examined and recorded by the heart of Heaven).

Mingjia (冥加) says regarding Xiaoheng: There are two kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). First is manifest empowerment (*pratyakṣādhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to manifesting body and speech to offer praise and seal one’s actions.
Second is hidden empowerment (*parokṣādhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to secretly bestowing protection and guidance without manifesting body or speech.
The Prince of the Śyāmaka Demons, named *Āditya*, had a father who was afflicted by illness.
A physician declared that only human eyes would suffice for the cure. Thereupon, he gouged out his own eyes to save his father.
The Youth of Compassion, out of a compassionate heart, once cut a single strand of his mother’s hair; he consequently fell into the Hell of the Wheel of Fire.
There, seeing all the sinners undergoing immeasurable suffering, he immediately made this vow: "Whatever they endure, I shall take it all upon myself. Having uttered this vow, the fire...
The wheel then ceased.
Zeng Shen, Min Dun, and Mencius said:

"When Zengzi was caring for Zeng Xi, there were always wine and meat. When they were about to be removed, he would invariably ask where they should be given away. He would inquire whether there was [any left]."
[If] there were leftovers, he would certainly say there were. When Zeng Xi died, Zeng Yuan was nursing Zengzi. There was always wine and meat;
when they were about to be removed, [Zeng Yuan] did not ask where it could be given away. When asked if there were any leftovers, he said, "There are none," intending to serve them again.
This is what is called nourishing the mouth and body. As for Zengzi, however, he may be said to have nourished the will. Min Dun, styled Ziqian, lost his mother early. His father remarried.

The wife gave birth to two sons. She clothed them in cotton wool; when the clothing was worn out, she used reed flowers instead. The father ordered Sun (損) to drive the carriage, but his body being cold, he lost the leather thong.
The father observed this and learned of the situation, wishing to expel the stepmother. Sun said, "If the mother remains, one son may be cold; if the mother leaves, all three sons will be destitute.
Upon hearing this, the mother repented and changed her ways.
Great Shun and Lai Zi.

Yu Shun’s father was obstinate and his mother was garrulous, while his brother Xiang was arrogant; yet he was able to harmonize them through filial piety, serving them with ever-increasing reverence so that they did not resort to wickedness.
Lao Lai Zi served his two parents with filial devotion; having reached the age of seventy, fearing that his parents might worry because of his old age, he dressed himself in five-colored garments.
Wearing variegated garments, he played like an infant; he would often take water up to the hall, then feign a fall to the ground, crying like a small child.
He would dally with the young birds by his parents' side, wishing to bring them joy and forgetting that he was old.
King Wen and Xue Bao.

When King Wen served as the heir apparent, he attended upon King Ji three times each day. At the first crowing of the cock, he went outside the door of the inner quarters and asked the attendants, "How is His Majesty’s well-being this day?
The palace page replied, "He is well. King Wen was then pleased. This continued until noon.
He arrived again at the same time the next day, and at evening he arrived again, likewise. Whenever there was anything that troubled him, King Wen’s countenance would show his anxiety;
he could not walk straight, nor could he keep his steps steady. Xue Bao was fond of learning and devoted to practice.

His father took a later wife who came to hate Bao and drove him out. Bao wept day and night, unable to leave. Even when he was subjected to beatings with a staff, he had no choice but to dwell in a hut outside the house.
At dawn he entered to sweep and sprinkle water. His father became angry and drove him away again. He then built a hut at the village gate, never ceasing his duties morning and evening.
After more than a year had passed, his parents felt ashamed and sent him back.

In praising filial piety, Confucius said: "The former kings possessed the most essential and comprehensive Way to bring harmony to the world; thus the people lived in concord, and there was no resentment between those above and below.
He further said: "How profound! How great is filial piety! What could the virtue of a sage possibly surpass filial piety?"
Ah! Nature and destiny, as well as filial piety and fraternal duty, are discussed as a single matter.
The *Lunyu* states: "When the Master spoke of nature (*xing*), it was not something that could be questioned; as for destiny (*ming*), it was something the Master rarely spoke of."
Indeed, the Way of Yao and Shun consists simply in filial piety and fraternal respect; outside of nature and destiny (*xingming*), there is no such thing as filial piety and fraternal respect.
Sijing Xiaoheng said: "Parents possess the grace of giving birth and raising one; therefore, one must be filial and obedient. Teachers and monks possess the grace of instruction and guidance..."

Because there is grace; therefore, one should be filial and obedient. The Three Jewels possess the grace of deliverance; thus, one must be filial and obedient. The Dharma of the Ultimate Way is the *dharmatā* of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because it is free from transgressions and is in accord with reality, it is called "filial obedience. Thus, the four realms were opened, but they are not employed now.
"Lowering one's breath and softening one's voice":

the *Nei ze* says, "When parents have faults, one lowers one's breath, softens one's countenance, and offers gentle words as counsel. If the counsel is not accepted, one redoubles one's reverence and filial piety."

The *Qu-lǐ* (Book of Ceremonial Etiquette) states: "In all the rites for one who is a son, he provides warmth in winter and coolness in summer; he settles his parents at dusk and visits them in the morning.
This is profound love."
The *Quli* says: "A filial son who possesses profound love will necessarily possess a harmonious air; one who possesses a harmonious air will necessarily possess a joyful countenance;
and one who possesses a joyful countenance will necessarily possess a gracious demeanor."

Zongmu said, "In their youth, people long for their parents; when they become aware of their desire for beauty, they long for young and lovely women; when they have wives and children, they long for their wives and children;

when they serve in office, they long for their ruler. When they do not find favor with their ruler, they feel a burning distress within. Only the great filial son longs for his father throughout his entire life."
"Regarding 'the mother'—one who cherishes her at the age of fifty—we see this in the case of the Great Shun.
Le Zhengzichun said, "In every step he takes, he does not dare to forget his parents; in every word he utters, he does not dare..."

The master went to visit him to provide guidance; the spirit manifested his true form as a massive python and shed tears like rain. The following day, after the python had perished in the forest, he subsequently attained liberation.
The Dharma Gate of Releasing Ocean Fish:

Formerly, the Zen Master Zhizhe established a pond for releasing living beings on the seashore. Whenever he released them, he invariably conferred upon them the precepts of refuge and expounded the Great Dharma.
After the passing of Master Zhizhe, by the end of the Tang dynasty, the Way of Tiantai had declined in China. However, [the tradition]...
This teaching was widely propagated in the various kingdoms of Goryeo and Silla to the east of the sea. Master Jizhong said:

"Since Zhiyi’s karmic conditions lay in this region, yet his teachings were spread to the east of the sea, these must surely be those fish in the pond for releasing life who heard the teachings and were reborn as a result."
A flying bird was a disciple, and a pheasant listened as the Dharma Master preached the Lotus Sūtra. Later, they died and were reborn among humans to become disciples of their former teacher.
[This concludes] the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* on Non-duality.
Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "What is the bodhisattva’s entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality?

Mañjuśrī replied, "It is that which is without speech and without expression, transcending all questioning and answering; this is non-duality. Mañjuśrī then questioned Vimalakīrti again, whereupon Vimalakīrti remained silent.

When Bai Juyi was serving as the Governor of Hangzhou, he entered the mountains to visit Chan Master Niaokuo and asked, "Where is the Chan Master’s dwelling?"

“It is very perilous,” the Master said. The official replied, “My position as Governor is even more perilous than that. The Master asked, “You sit in command over mountains and rivers; what peril could there be? The Master continued, “When fuel and fire intersect, the nature of consciousness does not rest—is this not perilous? The official then asked, “What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

The Master replied, “Commit no evil; practice all good deeds. The official remarked, “Even a three-year-old child knows that. The Master said, “A three-year-old child may indeed know it, but an eighty-year-old man cannot put it into practice. The official was deeply moved and subsequently became a monk under the Master. He later built a temple at Mount Lu and named it Baofeng (Treasure Peak).

It is said that he attained the Way after practicing for twenty years. His stupa is located at the foot of the mountain. Later generations call it the Baofeng Temple. It is still in existence today. This concludes the biography of National Teacher Huizhong.

The Fourth Patriarch, Great Master Daoxin of the Tang, did not return despite three imperial summons. In the year of Guimao during the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong, drawn to the flavor of the Master’s Way and wishing to behold his dignified presence, issued an edict for him to come to the capital.
The Master submitted a memorial declining the invitation; though he repeated this three times, he ultimately declined on the grounds of illness. This was the fourth [summons].

The messenger of the Emperor of Du-ming said, "If you do not rise, I shall take your head. When the messenger arrived at the mountain and delivered the imperial decree, Huizang drew out his neck to meet the blade;

his countenance remained solemn and composed. The messenger was struck with wonder and returned to report the circumstances to the Emperor. The Emperor’s admiration increased all the more, and he bestowed precious silks upon him so that his resolve might be fulfilled.
